Brain Connectivity

If the brain functions are segmented into different physical areas of the brain, how do they join up and communicate? Specialised regions handle different parts of the problem, and connectivity (tracts, hubs, neuromodulators, rhythms) allows them to operate as a single, adaptive system for perception and memory.

The brain coordinates specialised regions through white‑matter tracts, relay hubs (e.g., thalamus), neuromodulators (dopamine, acetylcholine), and oscillatory synchrony (theta–gamma coupling). Memory reconstruction depends on these channels to re‑activate and integrate distributed traces.

Key Tracts and Hubs

Structure Connects Role in Memory Integration Example
Corpus callosum Left ↔ Right hemispheres Interhemispheric binding of features and language–vision coordination Face seen left visual field, name retrieved from left language areas
Cingulum bundle Medial PFC ↔ Posterior cingulate ↔ Parahippocampal Default Mode Network integration; episodic context Linking self‑relevant cues to scene recall
Uncinate fasciculus Anterior temporal (semantic, amygdala) ↔ Orbitofrontal Emotion–meaning–decision coupling Affective tone biases what detail is retrieved
Thalamus Widespread cortical loops Relay/gating; timing alignment across areas Coordinating sensory evidence with retrieval attempts

Large‑Scale Networks

Network Nodes (Typical) Function Memory Role
Default Mode Network (DMN) mPFC, PCC/precuneus, angular gyrus, hippocampus Self‑projection, scene construction Reconstruct episodic scenes, imagine futures
Salience Network Anterior insula, dACC Detect importance; switch networks Selects what gets encoded/retrieved
Central Executive Network DLPFC, posterior parietal Working memory, control Guides search, monitors accuracy
